stem: Why should mucous membranes and conjunctiva be checked rather than skin complexion alone when assessing a child for anaemia?

options.text: Skin complexion can be misleading due to natural paleness or general illness
Jaundice is only visible in the mucous membranes
Skin colour only changes in acute blood loss
Red blood cells do not circulate near the skin surface in children
Conjunctival colour is unaffected by haemoglobin level

explanation: Skin complexion can be misleading because a child may be naturally fair or appear pale from general illness even when haemoglobin is normal. Checking the mucous membranes and conjunctiva gives a more reliable assessment of anaemia.

optionExplanations.A: Correct because skin complexion can be misleading due to natural paleness or general illness, so it is a less reliable sign of anaemia.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because jaundice can be seen in the sclera and other tissues, but that is not the reason mucous membranes and conjunctiva are preferred for anaemia assessment.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because skin colour may be affected in both acute and chronic illness, and it is not limited to acute blood loss.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because red blood cells do circulate near the skin surface; the issue is that skin colour is an unreliable marker because of natural complexion and illness-related pallor.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because conjunctival colour can reflect haemoglobin level and is therefore useful when assessing for anaemia.

source.hint: Consider factors like ethnicity, natural coloring, and how the body reacts to general illness beyond blood count.
